t: Check if it is Possible to Split Array
o: Repeatedly split arrays into two 'good' parts (length 1, or sum ≥ m) until all pieces are singletons. Surprising simplification: the answer is YES iff n == 1 or some adjacent pair sums to ≥ m. Why necessary: trace the splits backwards — merging singletons, the last merge that produced a multi-element piece required a good part of length ≥ 2, ultimately forcing some adjacent pair with sum ≥ m. Why sufficient: peel off single elements one at a time until only that good pair remains, then split it. Examples: [2,2,1], m=4 has pair (2,2) → true; [2,1,3], m=5 has pairs 3,4 → false.
k: Answer ⇔ n == 1 or ∃ adjacent i with nums[i] + nums[i+1] ≥ m.
Necessity comes from reversing the splitting process; sufficiency from peeling singles down to the good pair.
An interval DP over (sum ≥ m) subarrays also works and is a good fallback if the invariant is unclear.

a.i: Just scan for an adjacent pair with sum ≥ m (or n == 1). O(n) after proving the characterization.
s: Return whether any nums[i] + nums[i+1] ≥ m.
a.t: O(n) — single pass over adjacent pairs

a.i: dp[i][j] = can nums[i..j] be fully split. Base dp[i][i] = true. Transition: some cut k where the left piece is good (length 1 or sum ≥ m), the right piece is good, and both sides recursively splittable. Prefix sums give range sums in O(1); n ≤ 100 makes O(n³) fine.
s: Fill dp by increasing interval length, trying every cut.
a.t: O(n³) — all intervals × cuts with O(1) sums

w: In an interview, derive the adjacent-pair characterization — it turns a scary process problem into one line; keep the interval DP ready as verification/fallback. Pitfall: assuming a single large element (≥ m alone) suffices — it does not help split the rest unless adjacency holds somewhere. Follow-up: what if pieces had to be split in half, or m applied to averages?
